thread.title: Dow Rises 28 Points on Hopes for a U.S.-China Trade Deal

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Dow Rises 28 Points on Hopes for a U.S.-China Trade Deal
text:
Illustration: Agence France-Presse/Getty Images By Teresa Rivas Sept. 12, 2018 5:12 p.m. ET Trade Tango . Wednesday morning’s doldrums were quickly forgotten as s tocks gained steam on renewed hopes of trade negotiations between the U.S. and China. However, more semiconductor weakness and an underwhelming event from Apple (AAPL) kept tech stocks in the red. In today’s After the Bell , we….
parse trade hopes; hypothesize about interest rates, and; cringe at Micron Technology ’s (MU) slide. Hope Springs Eternal
Stocks skipped ahead on Wednesday as investors cheered news that the U.S. and China will try again to find a way forward on trade .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 27.86 points, or 0.11%, to 25,998.92 while the S&P 500 rose 1.03 points, or 0.04%, to 2888.92 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 18.24 points, or 0.23%, to 7954.23.
A positive outcome on tariffs couldn’t come at a better time. This afternoon, before the close, the Federal Reserve’s Beige Book revealed pockets of weaker growth , and trade was one of the main culprits. Along with worker shortages, additional tariffs were a major concern for businesses, the report noted, as three of the Fed’s 12 districts (Kansas City, Philadelphia, and St. Louis) reported weaker growth. East Coast ports haven’t been hurt by the trade restrictions, but are still worried, as long-lead times on shipping mean that the pain could still be coming. Any resolution to the ongoing trade spat would remove an overhang that investors would love to see disappear, even if it’s affecting overseas markets much more than home.
Still, the Beige Book probably pleased some, especially when taken with this morning’s producer price index reading, (which showed inflation looking largely in check), in terms of the Fed’s thinking, as neither were evidence of an economy heating up too quickly. (While the central bank seems committed to an interest-rate increase this month, a December hike is more hotly debated.)
Wells Fargo’s Jay Bryson thinks that ultimately we’ll get five more interest-rate increases (two this year, in September and December, and three next year), for a total of 125 basis points, before the Fed cuts rates at the end of 2020, on the heels of a more sluggish economy. He predicts gross domestic product will slip below a 2% annualized rate by the second half of 2020, prompting a 25 basis-point rate trim.
Yet even in a relatively benign environment investors can always find something to worry about. Commonwealth Financial Network’s Brad McMillan notes that the yield curve dropped a little bit further in August, bringing it to a new post-crisis low, although it’s still “well outside the trouble zone, so the immediate risk remains low.” Still, the spread’s decline, which inches it ever-closer to the (unjustifiably?) dreaded inversion, in combination with the Fed’s expected increases means that focus on the metric is likely to remain. “I am leaving this measure at a green light for now, but you can see a shade of yellow.”
Still, investors don’t seem much concerned today, and even if the next bear market comes, they should welcome it, says DataTrek’s Nicholas Colas . “The last 20 years have taught us all one thing: bear markets drive long-term performance at least as much as up markets.” Recessions are inevitable, but recoveries follow, and at present, “markets discount only garden-variety recessions and manageable bear markets over the next 10 years.” The S&P 500 has more than doubled in the past decade, leaving every other major equity market in the dust, thanks to relentless innovation. His conclusion: S&P 6000 will get here, one way or another.
The Hot Stock
Discovery (DISCA) shot to the top of the S&P 500 on Wednesday, on news that its inked a multiyear deal with Hulu and positive commentary from its CEO.
Discovery gained $2.19, or 7.7%, to $30.70. The company’s class C shares were the second biggest winner, rising $1.90, or 7.2%, to $28.36.
The deal with Hulu will see five new Discovery networks, including the Discovery Channel, available to Hulu subscribers, beginning in December. Discovery’s CEO also reaffirmed the company’s full-year guidance during an interview with CNBC, and said that advertising growth will accelerate in the third and fourth quarters.
Year to date, Discovery has risen 37.2%, and it’s up 46.2% in the past 12 months.
The top five stocks in the S&P 500:
Discover Class A (DISCA): 7.7%
Discover Class C (DISCK): 7.2%
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): 7%
Altria Group (MO): 6.7%
Freeport-McMoRan (FCX): 4.5%
The Biggest Loser
Micron Technology tumbled to the bottom of the index, hurt by a downgrade from Goldman Sachs .
Micron lost $1.86, or 4.3%,t o $41.74.
Goldman Sachs’ Mark Delaney downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy, and lowered his price target on the shares to $50 from $60, warning that he sees weaker fundamentals for DRAM and NAND memory ahead. He also lowered his price target on Western Digital (WDC) to $63 from $80 and on Seagate Technology (STX) to $39, from $44, while reiterating Neutral and Sell ratings on those stocks, respectively, also on memory concerns.
Micron is up 1.5% year to date, and it’s added 21.7% in the past 12 months.
The bottom five stocks in the S&P 500:
Micron Technology (MU): -4.3%
SunTrust Banks (STI): -3.8%
Twitter (TWTR): -3.7%
Comerica (CMA): -3.4%
Lam Research (LRCX): -3.2%
